Dear Vandana,
You were right when you said I keep circling the thing I want. I want to lead the new regional team. I've wanted it since my first week. But when Mr Sangma asked who would present the budget review to the board, I stared at my notebook until someone else raised a hand.
The truth is, I'm scared that if I try and fumble, everyone will see I'm not as good as they think. Not trying keeps the dream safe. It also keeps it far away.
So I'm trying your idea of small bets. On Friday I'll present just the first slide at our team meeting. Next month, one section at the board review. If my voice shakes, I'll survive it, and then I'll know.
I'll write and tell you how Friday goes.
Lalremsiami

Ritu, I'll tell you what happened, but don't laugh. You know I've always said I want to lead the city desk someday. Big stories, my name on top. And for two years I pitched nothing. Nothing! Every Monday meeting I sat with three story ideas in my notes and said, 'I'll support whoever's on it.'
Last month I finally saw why. If I pitch and it flops, I'm just someone who wanted too much. If I never pitch, I can keep believing I'd be brilliant.
So I made a deal with myself: one small pitch a week. Tiny ones. A leaking water tank in a school. The editor took it and said, 'Good one, Himani.' Then a story about night-shift bus drivers. She took that too.
It's not the city desk. But now I have proof, not just hope. My hands still shake on Mondays, though.

qa.q: What was Himani's first small pitch?
qa.a: A leaking water tank in a school.

qa.q: Why did Himani avoid pitching for two years?
qa.a: Himani feared that a flop would mean being someone who wanted too much, while never pitching kept the belief in being brilliant safe.

qa.q: What choice helped Himani move past the fear, and why did it work?
qa.a: A deal of one small pitch a week; each accepted story built real proof, not just hope.

qa.q: How might the editor see Himani now compared with before?
qa.a: The editor may now see Himani as someone with ideas worth running, rather than a quiet supporter who never pitched.

grounding: Shows a young professional whose wish for a big role is held back by fear of failing, until small weekly risks start building evidence.

passage: Saurabh, you remind me of myself at twenty-four. I wanted to be head chef so badly I could taste it. But whenever the kitchen needed someone to plan a new menu, I'd find something urgent to chop. What if my dishes flopped in front of everyone? Old Chef Mathew noticed. He didn't lecture. He said, "Tejas, Wednesday's staff lunch is yours. Only staff. If it's terrible, we eat biscuits." I, Tejas, was sick with nerves. The dal was too salty. The rice was perfect. People ate. The next month he gave me one dish on the real menu. Then two. Small risks, beta. Each one gives you proof that failing a little won't finish you.

qa.a: The staff lunch.

qa.a: He likely saw real talent held back by fear, and chose a gentle way to push.

The client pitch had moved up to Thursday, and the team was short-staffed. At 6 p.m. on Monday, Payal stopped by Noor's desk. "I want you to lead the pitch. You know this client best."
Noor's heart jumped. She had wanted to lead a pitch for two years; she'd told her mentor she wanted to be a team head someday. But her mouth said, "Maybe Arjit should do it. I'm not sure I'm ready."
Payal waited. "What's the worst thing that happens?"
"I freeze. They hate it. Everyone sees."
"Then take one piece. The opening five minutes. I'll do the rest."
Noor swallowed. Five minutes felt survivable. She rehearsed on the office stairwell that night and again on Wednesday morning.
On Thursday her voice shook for the first minute, then steadied. Afterwards, the client asked a question directly to her. She answered it.

qa.q: Which part of the pitch did Payal suggest Noor lead?
qa.a: The opening five minutes.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when Payal offered her the pitch?
qa.a: She felt excited and afraid at once: her heart jumped because she wanted it, but she dreaded freezing in front of everyone.

qa.q: Why did taking just the opening five minutes help Noor?
qa.a: It was a small, survivable risk that gave her real evidence she could do it, helping break the stalemate between wanting and dreading.

qa.q: How might Payal see Noor's first answer, "Maybe Arjit should do it"?
qa.a: Payal seems to see it as fear rather than lack of ability, so she gently asks about the worst case and offers a smaller step.
